cards.title: Sample-efficient latent-tree Ising learning
cards.formal: Can a polynomial-time algorithm properly learn a latent-tree Ising distribution in total variation distance using the information-theoretically required number of samples? The source concerns improving sample efficiency of an already polynomial-time learning procedure. Its conference wording asks for \(O(n/\varepsilon^{2})\) samples, but that literal bound conflicts with its stated unknown-topology lower bound. The source discrepancy and remaining precision choices are recorded below.

cards.why: Asks whether hidden variables create a computational cost in the number of observations needed to learn a distribution, even on trees. Distinguishing this question from topology identification and from ordinary statistical lower bounds is essential for interpreting a possible statistical-computational gap.

The conference question literally asks for \(O(n/\varepsilon^{2})\) samples, while its own Appendix E states an information-theoretic \(\Omega(n\log n/\varepsilon^{2})\) lower bound when the topology is unknown. The July 2023 full author version instead asks broadly about a statistical-computational gap after describing the sample rate up to logarithmic factors. A complete remaining target must select known versus unknown topology and specify whether it asks for the optimal rate up to constants or allows stated logarithmic factors. It must output another tree model with nearly the same joint distribution on those leaves.

cards.definitions:
A latent-tree Ising model has a finite undirected tree \(T=(V,E)\) whose \(n\geq2\) leaves are labeled \(1,\ldots,n\). Only leaf spins are observed; internal spins are hidden. Each edge \(e\) has a real correlation parameter \(\theta_{e}\in[-1,1]\). There are no external fields and no assumptions keeping edge correlations away from zero or from either endpoint.

One equivalent definition of its distribution is to root the tree anywhere, draw the root spin uniformly from \(\{-1,1\}\), and generate each child's spin independently conditional on its parent, with
\[\Pr[X_{v}=X_{u}\mid X_{u}]=(1+\theta_{\{u,v\}})/2.\]
Thus correlations may be positive, negative, zero or deterministic. The observed distribution \(P\) is the marginal on the \(n\) labeled leaves. Internal degree-two paths can be suppressed, and higher-degree nodes can be split using correlation-one edges, without changing \(P\). One can therefore use trees with degree-three internal nodes and linearly many vertices.

The learner receives independent samples from \(P\), each an entire vector in \(\{-1,1\}^{n}\). It receives no hidden spins or conditional-sampling oracle. The known-topology version additionally supplies the whole tree \(T\), but not its edge parameters. In the unknown-topology version both the tree and its parameters are hidden. The source discusses both versions.

Proper learning asks for an explicit tree Ising model with the same labeled observed leaves, whose induced leaf distribution \(\widehat P\) obeys
\[\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat P)=\frac12\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^{n}}|P(x)-\widehat P(x)|\leq\varepsilon.\]
The success probability is at least \(1-\delta\), over the samples and any internal algorithmic randomness. The recovered hidden topology and parameters need not equal the original ones; distributional accuracy on all leaves is the requirement. Pairwise-marginal accuracy alone, exact structure recovery and testing whether two supplied sample sources are close are separate goals.

A computationally efficient learner must use time polynomial in the dimension and accuracy parameters, with the cost of reading samples and writing a finite model description counted. For a precise benchmark one can state the sample rate at a fixed constant confidence, such as \(2/3\), and give explicit parameter and output encodings. The outstanding substantive choice here is the sample rate and topology information, not mere existence of a polynomial-time learner.

In the source's notation, a tilde over asymptotic bounds suppresses logarithmic factors. The ordinary \(O(n/\varepsilon^{2})\) bound printed in the conference question does not suppress them. The distinction affects whether the requested bound is even statistically possible for unknown topology.
cards.answer_criterion: First specify the topology-information setting and the allowed logarithmic dependence in the sample target, consistently with the information-theoretic bounds. A positive answer must give a proper learner satisfying the entire chosen sample, runtime and distributional-accuracy guarantee. A computational lower bound must state its assumptions. Failure of a sample bound already ruled out without computational restrictions is not evidence of a statistical-computational gap.

context_blocks.title: Polynomial-time proper learning is already available
context_blocks.text: The conference Theorem 3 uses \(O(n^{4}\log(n/\delta)/\varepsilon^{2})\) samples for known topology and \(O(n^{14}\log(n/\delta)/\varepsilon^{6})\) for unknown topology. These are the source’s proved historical bounds, rather than the missing open question. The nearby prose abbreviates the accuracy dependence and should not replace the theorem.

context_blocks.title: The statistical benchmark includes logarithms
context_blocks.text: Appendix E gives an information-theoretic upper bound \(O(n\log(n/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon^{2})\) at constant confidence and states an unknown-topology lower bound \(\Omega(n\log n/\varepsilon^{2})\). It cites Koehler’s minimax lower bound and its extension to latent trees. The lower bound does not assume an efficient learner. Consequently, the literal conference \(O(n/\varepsilon^{2})\) request cannot serve as an unknown-topology open target.

context_blocks.title: The full version avoids that literal request
context_blocks.text: The July 2023 full author discussion summarizes the information-theoretic rate as \(\widetilde\Theta(n/\varepsilon^{2})\), then asks whether a statistical-computational gap exists. It does not include the conference’s ordinary-\(O\) sentence. This supports the sample-efficiency motivation, but does not fix which logarithmic precision this card should demand.

context_blocks.title: New fully observed Ising guarantees have a different input
context_blocks.text: The 2026 COLT paper gives efficient total-variation learning guarantees under interaction-matrix and functional-inequality assumptions, using samples of every spin. Marginalizing hidden nodes does not in general leave an Ising model on the observed variables. These theorems do not resolve unrestricted learning from leaf-only samples.

cards.context:
The conference Theorem 3 uses \(O(n^{4}\log(n/\delta)/\varepsilon^{2})\) samples for known topology and \(O(n^{14}\log(n/\delta)/\varepsilon^{6})\) for unknown topology. These are the source’s proved historical bounds, rather than the missing open question. The nearby prose abbreviates the accuracy dependence and should not replace the theorem.

Appendix E gives an information-theoretic upper bound \(O(n\log(n/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon^{2})\) at constant confidence and states an unknown-topology lower bound \(\Omega(n\log n/\varepsilon^{2})\). It cites Koehler’s minimax lower bound and its extension to latent trees. The lower bound does not assume an efficient learner. Consequently, the literal conference \(O(n/\varepsilon^{2})\) request cannot serve as an unknown-topology open target.

The July 2023 full author discussion summarizes the information-theoretic rate as \(\widetilde\Theta(n/\varepsilon^{2})\), then asks whether a statistical-computational gap exists. It does not include the conference’s ordinary-\(O\) sentence. This supports the sample-efficiency motivation, but does not fix which logarithmic precision this card should demand.

The 2026 COLT paper gives efficient total-variation learning guarantees under interaction-matrix and functional-inequality assumptions, using samples of every spin. Marginalizing hidden nodes does not in general leave an Ising model on the observed variables. These theorems do not resolve unrestricted learning from leaf-only samples.
